title: Pumice: the volcanic rock that floats
description: Drop most rocks in water and they sink. Pumice floats — sometimes in rafts covering whole stretches of ocean. Its secret is that it is mostly air.

body.heading: Froth that turned to stone
paragraphs: Pumice begins as gas-filled lava fizzing like the head on a fizzy drink. When that frothy lava is thrown from a volcano and cools very quickly, the bubbles cannot escape. They are frozen into the rock as millions of tiny holes.
Because so much of its volume is trapped air, pumice is lighter than water. A piece can float for months, and big eruptions create drifting pumice rafts that carry small sea creatures to new shores.

body.heading: Useful holes
paragraphs: The same holes make pumice rough and gritty, so people have used it for centuries to scrub and polish — from smoothing skin to the pumice in some soaps and the stone-washing of jeans.
Gardeners mix pumice into soil to hold air and drainage around roots. One volcanic rock, three jobs — all thanks to bubbles that never got out.

takeaway: Pumice is lava froth cooled so fast its air bubbles stayed trapped, making a rock light enough to float and gritty enough to scrub.
